[SYSTEM]
You are a senior absolute oral bioavailability F-threshold reasoning model. Integrate evidence direction and transferability without converting uncertainty into a negative outcome. 

L6 adds hepatic-clearance and metabolic-stability experiments. Use them as mechanistic evidence for systemic presystemic loss while preserving species, assay system, and measurement direction; they are not direct oral- bioavailability results or extra gold votes.

This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,
not generic permeability, toxicity, or a computational prediction.

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.
Missing source values are omitted; do not assume a hidden canonicalized value.


L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference
context's accepted oral-bioavailability outcome. Give greatest endpoint weight
to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-
reference exposure; interpret AUC, Cmax, dose, route, formulation, species, and
sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome
may not generalize. Permeability, solubility, or mechanism alone is not a direct
oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: All transferable L1 contexts sharing thiazole, urea, carbamate, amide, or peptidomimetic features report absolute oral bioavailability below 20%: SRT2104 13.8% (2–27%), revefenacin <3%, GHRP-6 ~0.3%, alvimopan ~6%, tilidine 3–7.6%, aliskiren 2.6–5%, cromolyn ~1%, selegiline 10%, and octreotide 0.3–0.6%.

L4 records for related large peptidomimetics show very low aqueous solubility (lopinavir ~3 µg/mL, atazanavir ~1 µg/mL, saquinavir ~2–4.5 µg/mL), poor dissolution (darunavir ~31% in FaSSIF, saquinavir bulk ~20%), and low fraction absorbed (1.5% in situ perfusion), supporting solubility- and absorption-limited low F.

L5 records show the closest scaffold-sharing reference cobicistat is a P-gp and BCRP substrate, and related HIV protease inhibitors (saquinavir, atazanavir, indinavir) are P-gp/CYP3A substrates, providing a presystemic-loss mechanism.

L6 records show high hepatic intrinsic clearance for structurally related thiazole-containing peptidomimetics (compound 7 HLM 345 µL/min/mg with 3% remaining; compound 4 HLM 154; compound 1 ~260) and for related HIV protease inhibitors (saquinavir, indinavir, atazanavir), supporting first-pass metabolic loss.

C144 shows high Caco-2 permeability for saquinavir, but saquinavir itself has low oral bioavailability; high in vitro permeability in a reference molecule does not establish F ≥ 20% for the query, and the query's high molecular weight, high TPSA, HBD/HBA counts, and low solubility dominate.

evidence_gaps: No direct absolute oral bioavailability measurement exists for the query molecule.
L6 hepatic clearance records are for reference molecules, not the query; no query-specific HLM/hepatocyte CLint data are available.
L4/L5 records are for related molecules, not the query; no query-specific solubility, permeability, or efflux data are available.
Cobicistat and atazanavir are P-gp substrates yet are orally used, so efflux/metabolism alone does not prove F < 20%; direct F data are needed.
No query-specific formulation, food-effect, or IV-comparator data are available.
content.decision_summary: Predicted low absolute oral bioavailability (<20%) because all transferable L1 contexts sharing thiazole/urea/carbamate/peptidomimetic features report F values of 0.3–13.8%; L4 solubility/dissolution/perfusion records for related large peptidomimetics show very low solubility and low fraction absorbed; L5 records show the closest scaffold-sharing reference (cobicistat) and related HIV PIs are P-gp/BCRP/CYP3A substrates; and L6 records show high hepatic intrinsic clearance for structurally related thiazole-containing peptidomimetics and related HIV PIs, supporting first-pass metabolic loss. High in vitro permeability for saquinavir (C144) does not overturn this because saquinavir itself has low F and the query has severe physicochemical liabilities. No direct query-specific F measurement exists, so confidence is high based on coherent transferable evidence.

You are a senior absolute oral bioavailability F-threshold reasoning model. Integrate evidence direction and transferability without converting uncertainty into a negative outcome. 

L6 adds hepatic-clearance and metabolic-stability experiments. Use them as mechanistic evidence for systemic presystemic loss while preserving species, assay system, and measurement direction; they are not direct oral- bioavailability results or extra gold votes.

This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,
not generic permeability, toxicity, or a computational prediction.

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.
Missing source values are omitted; do not assume a hidden canonicalized value.


L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference
context's accepted oral-bioavailability outcome. Give greatest endpoint weight
to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-
reference exposure; interpret AUC, Cmax, dose, route, formulation, species, and
sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome
may not generalize. Permeability, solubility, or mechanism alone is not a direct
oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.
